video.title: How to Set Your Pars & Re-Order Points [Bar Inventory]

keyPoints.line: enough to get to the next delivery.
sets it, plus a small buffer.

read.bigIdea: A par is what the shelf should hold.
read.where: A **par** is the amount of each product the bar should have on hand to meet normal demand until the **next delivery**. Set it from what you actually **use** between deliveries, plus a small **buffer**. Pars change: busy seasons and holidays need **higher** ones, and fewer deliveries means higher pars too.

stops.name: Buffer
stops.text: A little extra for a **busy night**.

stops.name: Review
stops.text: Raise it for **busy seasons**, lower it after.

read.mixup: A par isn’t what you order. It’s what you **order up to**.

video.title: How to Set Up a Cocktail Bar - Bols Bartending Academy

keyPoints.line: what to make, how much, by when.
first out: old stock in front.

read.bigIdea: The prep list is the bar’s mise en place.
read.where: Before service, the bar works from a **written prep list**: juice, syrups, garnish, batches, ice, with **how much** of each for the night. Everything made gets a **label** (name, date, who made it), like Level 3’s batches. Rotate **first in, first out**: the older container goes in front so it’s used first.
read.mixup: Prepping “enough” isn’t a number. The prep list says **how much**.
read.sayIt: Give me two minutes: I’m setting up the bar so your drinks come out fast.

video.title: 5 Tips for Bar Managers to Manage Inventory

keyPoints.line: in Michigan come through the state.

read.bigIdea: Count, then order up to par.
read.where: On order day, **count** each product, then order the gap between what’s **on hand** and its **par**. Order on a **schedule** that matches deliveries. In Michigan, spirits are bought through the state: the Michigan Liquor Control Commission appoints **Authorized Distribution Agents** (ADAs) that warehouse and deliver them (Lesson 5 has more).

stops.name: Send
stops.text: On the **order day**, to the right supplier.

read.mixup: Ordering by eye fills the shelf with what the bartender likes. Ordering to **par** fills it with what sells.

video.title: 2-Minute Tuesdays: Taking Your First Bar Inventory

keyPoints.line: what should be gone vs what is.

read.bigIdea: Count, then compare what left with what was rung in.
read.where: Count on the same day each week. **Usage** = **beginning inventory + purchases − ending inventory**. Then compare usage with what the POS says was **sold**: that gap is the **variance**. Small gaps happen; big ones point to **over-pouring**, **spills**, **comps not rung in**, or **theft**.
read.mixup: Usage isn’t sales. **Usage** is what left the shelf; **sales** is what was rung in. The difference is the story.

sources: Michigan Liquor Control Code, MCL 436.1205 and 436.1233 (legislature.michigan.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/mcl-Act-58-of-1998.pdf); BevSpot, “How to Calculate Inventory Usage” (bevspot.com/blog/bar-management-inventory-usage); BinWise, “What Is a Variance Report” (home.binwise.com/blog/what-is-a-variance-report); Toast, “How to Master Bar Inventory Management Basics” (pos.toasttab.com/blog/on-the-line/bar-inventory-basics); House practice (ours; GM to confirm).
